body.text: A couple of months before the 2020 U.S. presidential election, former Deputy Assistant U.S. Trade Representative Glen Fukushima published an article in The Japan Times titled “Why Do Japan’s Leaders Prefer Republicans?” The purpose of the article was to explain why Japanese policymakers – particularly those associated with the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) – tend to favor a Republican president over a Democratic one.

Drawing on his own experience interacting directly with Japanese counterparts during his service in the Reagan administration, Fukushima argued that Japan’s leaders believe they have more in common with Republicans. These shared characteristics include conservative values, support for free trade, familiarity with Republican administrations – which held the U.S. presidency for a combined 28 years between 1980 and 2008 – and a perception that Republican administrations exert less pressure on Japan regarding cultural and social issues.

While much has changed since 2020, Fukushima’s portrayal of Japanese elites’ preference for Republican presidents over Democratic ones largely remains relevant. Although Trump’s first term was marked by political turmoil, a poorly managed global pandemic, and the January 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol, Japan’s leaders and conservative pundits nevertheless embraced a confrontational approach toward Beijing.

At the same time, Trump’s mercurial approach to trade and burden-sharing created friction with U.S. allies, yet Japanese leaders, notably Abe Shinzo and Takaichi Sanae, sought to navigate their relationship with their American counterpart strategically. As demonstrated by the relationships between Nakasone Yasuhiro and Ronald Reagan, and between Koizumi Junichiro and George W. Bush, LDP prime ministers have repeatedly demonstrated an ability to establish personal rapport with Republican presidents.

On the other hand, while the Biden administration struck a friendlier and more accommodating tone toward Japan than its predecessor, it also reinforced some of the worst stereotypes that Japanese conservatives held about Democratic administrations. Biden’s increasingly hawkish rhetoric toward China, including his repeated statements about defending Taiwan, was not always matched by commensurate increases in real defense spending, particularly during the early years of his administration.

Meanwhile, U.S. Ambassador to Japan Rahm Emanuel’s public campaign to encourage the Japanese Diet to pass legislation promoting understanding of LGBTQ people sparked considerable backlash among Japanese conservatives, who viewed his advocacy as an unwelcome intervention in Japan’s domestic affairs. Emanuel’s activism provided ammunition to conservatives already disillusioned with what they perceived as the LDP’s increasingly liberal direction, potentially encouraging some to shift their political allegiance toward smaller, more explicitly right-wing parties.

Another major disappointment for Japanese leaders during the Biden administration was its intervention to block Nippon Steel’s acquisition of U.S. Steel. Facing pressure from labor unions and seeking to maintain his image as the “most pro-union president,” Biden blocked the deal, citing “credible evidence” that the acquisition could “impair the national security of the United States.” The Japanese government reacted with dismay, arguing that it was incomprehensible for an ally that Japan expected to help protect it against shared threats to regard a Japanese investment as a potential national security threat.

Ultimately, Biden’s decision was reversed by the second Trump administration, which saw an opportunity to claim credit for boosting domestic manufacturing while being less constrained by organized labor. In this sense, Trump aligned more closely with Japanese leaders’ general perception of Republican presidents as being easier to deal with.

However, the latest midterm elections may give Japanese leaders pause in their perception that Democrats are inherently sanctimonious and beholden to labor unions and political activists. One of the notable features of the Democrats’ strong electoral performance was their emphasis on an economic populist message rather than positioning themselves primarily as defenders of established institutions or “universal values” – positions that can create distance between the party and ordinary voters. If cultural issues become less prominent in Democratic intraparty politics, this could offer hope not only for Japan but also for other Asian allies, many of which tend to be more socially conservative, by allowing them to engage with Washington without constantly feeling lectured about their domestic values and policies.

However, what matters more to Japan is whether Democrats will have sufficient political will and capacity to defend the country and help it counter external security threats. While economic populism may push social issues to the sidelines, it could instead bring other costly domestic priorities to the forefront, potentially pushing the revitalization of the U.S. defense industrial base further down the political agenda.

Moreover, the politicization of the war in Iran – particularly if Democrats seek to cut off funding to force the president to back down – could have unintended consequences for essential military investments needed to strengthen deterrence in theaters beyond the Middle East. Although Japan and other Asian allies might welcome a reduced U.S. military presence in the Middle East, Democrats would need to reassure them that they remain committed to prioritizing the Indo-Pacific, as they have repeatedly pledged, and that these commitments will be backed by credible military capabilities and sustained resources.

While U.S. allies may have a preference for one of the United States’ two major political parties, they must learn to work across the aisle. Regardless of whether Washington is governed by Republicans or Democrats, the value of existing treaty commitments remains unchanged. One of the key lessons of the latest U.S. midterm elections is that no political alignment is permanent: voters are willing to cross ideological lines, potentially signaling a broader realignment of party loyalties. Such realignments are hardly unprecedented; they have occurred repeatedly throughout the United States’ political history. Thus, the need to be flexible with either party in power is essential.

For Japan, getting along with Democrats will mean venturing into less familiar political and institutional circles, including universities, major metropolitan areas, think tanks, labor unions, technology hubs, and environmental policy networks. Such efforts are essential to establishing firm ties with emerging Democratic figures and influential actors outside government who may, over time, wield as much influence over policymaking as those formally responsible for implementing it. The controversy surrounding Nippon Steel’s proposed acquisition of U.S. Steel demonstrated the importance of these actors in shaping bilateral relations.

Ultimately, as former NATO Secretary-General Peter Carrington once observed, regardless of differences in political systems, for U.S. allies the current Americans in power “are the only Americans we have.” While continuing to strengthen its historically close ties with the Republican Party, Japan would be well served by building a robust network of relationships with Democratic leaders and influential constituencies. Such investments may prove valuable sooner than expected and are likely to pay dividends for decades to come.
